claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 can initially exist as a high-temperature BCC phase.
Annealing Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 above an order-disorder transition produces a homogenized BCC state.
Local atomic ordering in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is induced by atomic-size mismatch and chemical affinity between Al and transition metals, particularly Cr.
Local ordering involving differently sized atoms generates local strain or lattice-distortion fields.
Local ordering creates heterogeneous diffusion pathways in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Nanoscale compositional fluctuations and strain fields promote inhomogeneous nucleation of B2 or minor FCC regions from the BCC matrix.
The extent and morphology of ordering and phase evolution depend strongly on cooling rate and subsequent thermal exposure.
Slow cooling or intermediate-temperature aging provides sufficient diffusion for ordering, precipitation, or phase separation.
Atomic-size mismatch and Al-Cr chemical pairing create regions with low activation barriers for ordering.
Rapid water quenching suppresses local reordering and retains a largely homogeneous BCC state with minimal local ordering.
Relative to the water-quenched baseline, slowly cooled or aged Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 will contain detectable secondary ordered phases such as B2 and potentially minor FCC regions.
Secondary FCC regions can exhibit defined crystallographic orientation relationships with the parent BCC matrix.
The secondary phases in slowly cooled or aged samples will have local compositions distinguishable from the matrix.
The proposed mechanism applies when diffusion is moderately activated below the high-temperature BCC stability range but before complete homogenization.
The proposed mechanism should not produce secondary phases when cooling is sufficiently rapid to freeze atomic mobility or aging is insufficient.
High oxygen or nitrogen contamination or extreme nonequilibrium processing can obscure or dominate the proposed ordering behavior.
The identity, morphology, and volume fraction of secondary phases depend on intrinsic diffusion rates and local compositional fluctuations.

The hypothesis is falsified if slowly cooled or aged samples show neither statistically significant local ordering nor secondary phases relative to the quenched control, within experimental detection limits.
